Energ\\u00eda y de la Comisi\\u00f3n Reguladora Nuclear.\\n...\\nLa situaci\\u00f3n argentina es distinta porque el pa\\u00eds ya cuenta con ese marco desde hace casi tres d\\u00e9cadas. El acuerdo
fue firmado en Buenos Aires el 29 de febrero de 1996 y aprobado por el Congreso argentino mediante la Ley 24.862 en agosto de 1997. Por eso, la firma que el Ejecutivo proyecta para este a\\u00f1o no
debe confundirse con la entrada inmediata en vigencia del reemplazo.\\n...\\nDel lado estadounidense, los Acuerdos 123 deben atravesar adem\\u00e1s un procedimiento de revisi\\u00f3n en el Congreso
que totaliza 90 d\\u00edas de sesi\\u00f3n continua. Si el convenio cumple con las exigencias de no proliferaci\\u00f3n de la Acta de Energ\\u00eda At\\u00f3mica, puede entrar en vigor terminado ese
per\\u00edodo salvo que el Congreso apruebe una resoluci\\u00f3n conjunta para rechazarlo.\\n...\\nLa discusi\\u00f3n bilateral no se limita al marco jur\\u00eddico. En febrero, ambas delegaciones
destacaron su inter\\u00e9s en reactores modulares peque\\u00f1os -SMR- y otras tecnolog\\u00edas nucleares avanzadas, adem\\u00e1s de cooperaci\\u00f3n sobre regulaci\\u00f3n, licenciamiento,
protecci\\u00f3n f\\u00edsica, seguridad nuclear y ciberseguridad. La declaraci\\u00f3n oficial incluye expresamente el intercambio de informaci\\u00f3n t\\u00e9cnica en esas \\u00e1reas.\\n...\\nLa
agenda coincide con el inter\\u00e9s oficial por atraer capital estadounidense al sector nuclear argentino. En julio, el Gobierno present\\u00f3 la propuesta de Meitner Energy para desarrollar un
reactor modular de aproximadamente 300 MW en el complejo Atucha, con una inversi\\u00f3n privada estimada en US$1200 millones. La iniciativa todav\\u00eda debe atravesar aprobaciones y licenciamiento
y es independiente del Acuerdo 123, aunque refleja el tipo de participaci\\u00f3n empresarial que la Casa Rosada busca ampliar.\\n...\\nEn el Ejecutivo proyectan una l\\u00f3gica similar
en\\n...\\n\\u00e1reas espacial y satelital: acuerdos t\\u00e9cnicos, transferencia e intercambio de informaci\\u00f3n y una mayor participaci\\u00f3n de compa\\u00f1\\u00edas estadounidenses.
Argentina ya tiene una\\n...\\nArtemis II. La\\n...\\nCiberseguridad completa el paquete estrat\\u00e9gico que el Gobierno quiere profundizar con Washington. La Casa Rosada trabaja desde comienzos de
a\\u00f1o en un entendimiento destinado a obtener cooperaci\\u00f3n, tecnolog\\u00eda, equipamiento y programas de fortalecimiento de las capacidades estatales. El objetivo es aumentar la
prevenci\\u00f3n y respuesta ante ataques y proteger infraestructura cr\\u00edtica, en un esquema en el que Naci\\u00f3n prev\\u00e9 combinar acuerdos entre gobiernos, intercambio t\\u00e9cnico y

\"El Gobierno busca renovar su acuerdo nuclear con Estados Unidos antes de fin de a\\u00f1o | ANR\\n\\n# El Gobierno busca renovar su acuerdo nuclear con Estados Unidos antes de fin de
a\\u00f1o\\n\\nLa negociaci\\u00f3n qued\\u00f3 avanzada durante la reuni\\u00f3n del Comit\\u00e9 Permanente Conjunto de Cooperaci\\u00f3n en Energ\\u00eda Nuclear entre la Argentina y Estados Unidos
(JSCNEC), que se realiz\\u00f3 en Washington entre el 25 y el 27 de febrero.\\n\\n \\n\\nEl gobierno argentino se encuentra inmerso en la tarea de concretar un nuevo acuerdo de cooperaci\",
\"highlights\": [\"La negociaci\\u00f3n qued\\u00f3 avanzada durante la reuni\\u00f3n del Comit\\u00e9 Permanente Conjunto de Cooperaci\\u00f3n en Energ\\u00eda Nuclear entre la Argentina y Estados
Unidos (JSCNEC), que se realiz\\u00f3 en Washington entre el 25 y el 27 de febrero.\\n\\n \\n\\nEl gobierno argentino se encuentra inmerso en la tarea de concretar un nuevo acuerdo de
cooperaci\\u00f3n nuclear con Estados Unidos antes de concluir el a\\u00f1o. Este pretende sustituir el pacto que rige desde 1997, y que se encuentra pr\\u00f3ximo a su fecha de caducidad en 2027. En
los pasillos de la Casa Rosada, indican que los detalles t\\u00e9cnicos ya han sido finalizados y que lo que resta es la coordinaci\\u00f3n diplom\\u00e1tica a fin de efectuar la firma.\\n...\\nEsta
operaci\\u00f3n se sit\\u00faa bajo la normativa del Acuerdo Secci\\u00f3n 123 de la Acta de Energ\\u00eda At\\u00f3mica de los Estados Unidos. Este marco legal posibilita a los pa\\u00edses trabajar
en conjunto sobre energ\\u00eda nuclear con implicaciones civiles de envergadura. El anterior acuerdo fue sellado el 16 de octubre de 1997 con una vida \\u00fatil de 30 a\\u00f1os, y por consiguiente,
vence el pr\\u00f3ximo 16 de octubre.\\n...\\nLas negociaciones experimentaron una intensa evoluci\\u00f3n durante la reuni\\u00f3n del Comit\\u00e9 Permanente Conjunto de Cooperaci\\u00f3n en
Energ\\u00eda Nuclear, encuentro que reuni\\u00f3 a Argentina y Estados Unidos entre el 25 y 27 de febrero en Washington. La delegaci\\u00f3n argentina fue presidida por el secretario de Asuntos
Nucleares, Federico Ramos N\\u00e1poli, y fue escoltada por otras entidades relevantes del sector nuclear.\\n...\\nPercibido como un paso de notoria importancia, el convenio estipula el marco bajo el
cual pueden suceder traslaciones de tecnolog\\u00eda avanzada, equipamientos importantes, y en general materiales nucleares que Estados Unidos pueda exportar a otros Estados. Por s\\u00ed solo no
conlleva una adjudicaci\\u00f3n inmediata a ninguna compa\\u00f1\\u00eda ni loa adquisici\\u00f3n de reactores por parte del gobierno argentino.\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-08-10T00:00:00.000\",
\"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"Argentina sees exports as a key nuclear policy objective - World Nuclear News\", \"url\": \"https://world-nuclear-news.org/articles/argentina-sees-exports-as-key-
nuclear-policy-objective\", \"snippet\": \"Argentina sees exports as a key nuclear policy objective - World Nuclear News\\n\\n# Argentina sees exports as a key nuclear policy objective\\n\\n
Wednesday, 3 June 2026 \\n\\nThe four prioritised objectives for Argentina\\u2019s nuclear sector are \\\"high value-added exports, energy security, preservation and development of national
technological capacity, and regional leadership with geopolitical positioning\\\". \\n\\n(Image: CNEA)\\n\\nThe strategy was outlined in the Guidelines for the Argentine Nuclear Policy 2026 docu\",
\"highlights\": [\"Argentina sees exports as a key nuclear policy objective - World Nuclear News\\n\\n# Argentina sees exports as a key nuclear policy objective\\n\\n Wednesday, 3 June 2026 \\n\\nThe
four prioritised objectives for Argentina\\u2019s nuclear sector are \\\"high value-added exports, energy security, preservation and development of national technological capacity, and regional
leadership with geopolitical positioning\\\". \\n\\n(Image: CNEA)\\n...\\nThe strategy was outlined in the Guidelines for the Argentine Nuclear Policy 2026 document which was published as the country
marked the 76th anniversary of the founding of the National Atomic Energy Commission (CNEA).\\n...\\nAccording to C\\n...\\nPresident Martin Porro, writing about\\n...\\non social media site X:
\\\"For decades, the dispersion of efforts and the lack of a common direction postponed the true reach of the sector. Recognising those challenges clearly is not a step backward: it is what gives us
the right to build a new stage on solid foundations. We are not starting from zero. We have the infrastructure, the talent, and the projects to compete on the global stage. Our task is to organise
that potential and turn technical capacity into industry at scale.\\n...\\n\\\"We seek a virtuous circle, where the CNEA contributes research, development, and quality professionals, and companies
invest and assume the risk, under strict state oversight and fiscal discipline. Prestige is not proclaimed from nostalgia: it is sustained by putting all that potential into production. The world is
once again betting strongly on nuclear energy, and Argentina has what it takes to respond.\\\"\\n...\\nMeanwhile, Napoli, writing on X the week before the document was published, said that
\\\"reactivating uranium mining is a priority for this government\\\".\\n...\\n\\\"Argentina stopped extracting uranium in 1997, when operations ceased at the San Rafael Industrial Mining Complex
(Sierra Pintada, Mendoza). Since then, all the uranium that powers Atucha I-II and Embalse has been imported. Today the international context is the opposite of the 1990s. We are facing a springtime
of nuclear power generation on a global scale, and Argentina can not only become self-sufficient but also export and become a key player in the nuclear energy supply chain for the entire world,\\\" he
wrote.\\n...\\nHe added: \\\"Since January of this year, remediation efforts have been advancing at Sierra Pintada, the country's largest known uranium deposit, from which only 20% was extracted
throughout its entire production history. This is the prerequisite for resuming production. In parallel, mining projects in Chubut, R\\u00edo Negro, and Santa Cruz are starting to take their first
steps. The renewed global interest in nuclear energy is driving uranium demand. Argentina has reserves, expertise, and - for the first time in years - macroeconomic conditions that once again make it
profitable to invest in the country. The opportunity to complete the supply chain is real. We are going to reactivate uranium mining. And very soon.\\\"\"], \"published_date\":
\"2026-06-03T00:00:00.000\", \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"123 Agreements for Peaceful Cooperation - Department of Energy\", \"url\": \"https://www.energy.gov/nnsa/123-agreements-peaceful-
cooperation\", \"snippet\": \"123 Agreements for Peaceful Cooperation | Department of Energy\\n\\n# 123 Agreements for Peaceful Cooperation\\n\\nSection 123 of the U.S. Atomic Energy Act generally
requires the conclusion of a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement for significant transfers of nuclear material or equipment from the United States. Moreover, such agreements, commonly referred to
as \\u201c123 Agreements,\\u201d facilitate cooperation in other areas, such as technical exchanges, scientific research, and safeguards discussions. In c\", \"highlights\": [\"Section 123 of the U.S.
Atomic Energy Act generally requires the conclusion of a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement for significant transfers of nuclear material or equipment from the United States. Moreover, such
agreements, commonly referred to as \\u201c123 Agreements,\\u201d facilitate cooperation in other areas, such as technical exchanges, scientific research, and safeguards discussions. In conjunction
with other nonproliferation tools, particularly the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), 123 Agreements help to advance U.S. nonproliferation principles. These agreements
establish the legal framework for significant nuclear cooperation with other countries. In order for a partner to enter into a 123 Agreement with the United States, that partner must adhere to a set
of strong nonproliferation requirements. The U.S. Department of State is responsible for negotiating 123 Agreements, with the technical assistance and concurrence of DOE/NNSA and in consultation with
the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission.\\n...\\nAs of July 11, 2025, the United States has 26 such agreements in force that govern peaceful nuclear cooperation with 50 countries, the International
Atomic Energy Agency, and the governing authorities on Taiwan (through the American Institute in Taiwan), as detailed below.\\n...\\nUnited States Agreements for Cooperation Partners (entry into force
and expiration dates):\\n...\\n- Argentina (16 October 1997/16 October 2027)\\n- Australia (22 December 2010/22 December 2040 with rolling 5-year extensions)\\n- Brazil (15 September 1999/15 September
2029)\\n...\\n55/1\\n...\\n030\\n...\\n-year extensions)\\n...\\n- European Atomic Energy Community (Euratom)1 (12 April 1996/12 April 2026 with rolling 5-year extensions)\"], \"published_date\":

announces-privately-financed-smr-plan\", \"snippet\": \"Argentina announces privately-financed SMR plan - World Nuclear News\\n\\nHOME/ NEW NUCLEAR\\n\\n# Argentina announces privately-financed SMR
plan\\n\\nFriday, 10 July 2026\\n\\nArgentina's government has said US-based Meitner Energy is planning to invest USD1.2 billion in the construction of a 300 MW small modular reactor at the Atucha
site.\\n\\nArgentina's Economy Minister Luis Caputo and Federico Ramos Napoli, met Te\\u00f3filo Lacroze, CEO of Meitner Energy Latam, and Pablo Franzetti (image: @LuisCaputoAR/X)\\n\\nIn a p\",
\"highlights\": [\"Argentina announces privately-financed SMR plan - World Nuclear News\\n...\\n# Argentina announces privately-financed SMR plan\\n...\\nFriday, 10 July 2026\\n...\\nArgentina's
government has said US-based Meitner Energy is planning to invest USD1.2 billion in the construction of a 300 MW small modular reactor at the Atucha site.\\n...\\nIn a post on the X social media site
the President's Official Spokesman said: \\\"This is the first commercial version of this reactor, the first nuclear reactor financed 100% with private capital, and the largest investment in the
history of the Argentine nuclear sector.\\n...\\n\\\"The project envisions the creation of 2,000 direct jobs during the development, construction, commissioning, and operation stages, thereby
generating an expansion of the nuclear sector like never before. This investment is the result of the modernisation of the nuclear sector and the joint work of government authorities.\\\"\\n...\\nThe
proposal is to build an ACR-300 small modular reactor, which has been under development by Argentina's INVAP and which is described as using \\\"proven light\\u2011water technology ... [with the]
lowest physical construction burden per megawatt among grid\\u2011scale SMRs\\\".\\n...\\nSecretary of Nuclear Affairs Federico Ramos Napoli, also writing on X, said: \\\"Argentina has more than 70
years of nuclear track record, top-level institutions, and talent recognised worldwide. That a private company chooses our country to build its first reactor confirms that this technical capital, with
the right conditions, turns into investment, jobs, and baseload clean energy.\\\"\\n...\\nEconomy Minister Luis Caputo, posted a picture on X of the meeting with Meitner Energy executives (see above),
and said: \\\"The project will have an estimated investment of USD1.2 billion and will be funded through US private capital based on an Argentine patent. It involves the ACR-300, an SMR reactor of
Generation III+ and PWR technology, with an approximate power output of 300 MWe. This project will create around 2,000 direct jobs during the development, construction, commissioning, and operation
phases.\\\"\\n...\\nLast year's national nuclear plan for Argentina included four of the ACR-300 SMRs to be located at the Atucha Nuclear Power Plant site. It said at the time it expected that the
ACR-300 would have a construction timeline of five years.\\n...\\npower units - Atucha\\n...\\ns electricity. There\\n...\\nArgentina has already had an SMR in development: the CAREM SMR - the name
comes from Central Argentina de Elementos Modulares - a 32 MWe prototype and is Argentina's first domestically designed and developed nuclear power unit. First concrete was poured in 2014, but
construction has since been suspended a number of times, most recently when about two-thirds complete. Work on it is widely reported to be currently halted and the privately financed ACR-300 SMR was
described as \\\"the centrepiece of the Nuclear Power Plan\\\" last year.\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-07-10T00:00:00.000\", \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"Nuclear Cooperation with Other
Countries:\", \"url\": \"https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/RS/PDF/RS22937/RS22937.94.pdf\", \"snippet\": \"## Nuclear Cooperation with Other Countries:\\n\\n## A Primer\\n\\n##### Updated
February 10, 2026\\n\\nCongressional Research Service https://crsreports.congress.gov RS22937\\n\\nCongressional Research Service\\n\\n##### SUMMARY\\n\\n### Nuclear Cooperation with Other
Countries:\\n\\n### A Primer\\n\\nIn order for the United States to engage in significant civilian nuclear cooperation with other states, it must conclude a framework agreement that meets specific
requirements under Section 123 of the Atomic Energy Act (AEA). Si\", \"highlights\": [\"In order for the United States to engage in significant civilian nuclear cooperation with other states, it must
conclude a framework agreement that meets specific requirements under Section 123 of the Atomic Energy Act (AEA). Significant nuclear cooperation includes the export of reactors, critical parts of
reactors, and reactor fuel. The AEA also provides for export control licensing procedures and criteria for terminating cooperation. Congressional review is required for Section 123 agreements; the AEA
establishes special parliamentary procedures by which Congress may act on a proposed agreement.\\n...\\nUnder the Atomic Energy Act (AEA) of 1954, as amended (P.L. 83-703; 42 U.S.C. \\u00a72153 et
seq.), 1 all significant U.S. nondefense nuclear cooperation with other countries requires a nuclear cooperation agreement. 2 Significant nuclear cooperation includes the transfer of U.S.-origin
special nuclear material 3 subject to licensing for commercial, medical, and industrial purposes, and the export of reactors and critical parts of reactors. 4\\n...\\nSuch agreements, which are
\\u201ccongressional-executive agreements\\u201d requiring congressional review, set the terms of reference and authorize cooperation but do not guarantee that cooperation will take place. The Nuclear
Regulatory Commission (NRC) issues export licenses pursuant to Section 103 of the AEA. The AEA includes requirements for a Section 123 agreement\\u2019s content, conditions for the President to exempt
an agreement from those requirements, presidential determinations and other supporting information to be submitted to Congress, conditions affecting the implementation of an agreement once it takes
effect, and procedures for Congress to consider the agreement.\\n...\\nSection 123 of the AEA requires that any agreement for nuclear cooperation meet nine nonproliferation criteria and that the
President submit any such agreement to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs and the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations. The Department of State is required to provide the President with an
unclassified Nuclear Proliferation Assessment Statement (NPAS), which the President is to submit, along with the agreement, to those two committees. The State Department is also required to provide a
classified annex to the NPAS, prepared in consultation with the Director of National Intelligence. The NPAS is meant to explain the agreement\\u2019s compliance with the AEA nonproliferation
requirements. The President must also make a written determination \\u201cthat the performance of the proposed agreement will promote and will not constitute an unreasonable risk to, the common
defense and security.\\u201d In the case of a government that is not implementing an Additional Protocol to the government\\u2019s IAEA safeguards agreement, Section 1264 of the National Defense
Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2020 (P.L. 116-92) prohibits the President from providing to Congress an NPAS for a nuclear cooperation agreement. 5 This requirement is waived \\u201c90 days after
the date on which the President submits\\u201d to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and the House and Senate Armed Services Committees \\u201ca report
describing the manner in which such agreement would advance the national security and defense interests of the United States and not contribute to the proliferation of nuclear
weapons.\\u201d\\n...\\n123 of the AEA specifies the necessary steps for engaging in nuclear cooperation with another country.\\n...\\n\\u2022 Section 123a. states that the proposed agreement is to
include the terms, conditions, duration, nature, and scope of cooperation and lists nine criteria that the agreement must meet. This section also contains provisions for the President to exempt an
agreement from any of these criteria and specifies information the executive branch must provide to Congress.\\n...\\n123d\\n...\\nthe procedure for congressional review\\n...\\nagreements that
do\\n...\\nsignificant nuclear cooperation (transfer of nuclear material or reactors larger than 5 MWe), including exempted agreements. Section 123a.,\\n...\\n(1) through (9), lists nine criteria
that\\n...\\nagreement with a non-nuclear weapon state must meet unless the President determines an exemption is necessary. These include guarantees that\\n...\\nUnder the AEA, Congress has the
opportunity to review a nuclear cooperation agreement for two\\n...\\n90 days of continuous session.\\n...\\nPresident must submit\\n...\\nNPAS\\n...\\nForeign Affairs Committee\\n...\\nthe Senate
Foreign\\n...\\n| Argentina | | February 29, 1996 | | October 16, 1997 | 30 years | | October 16, 2027 | Extension by | |\\n...\\nSecurity Administration,\\n...\\n23\\n...\\nAgreements for Peaceful

UPI.com\", \"url\": \"https://www.upi.com/Top_News/World-News/2026/03/11/latam-argentina-nuclear-energy-partnerships/8591773244765/\", \"snippet\": \"Argentina seeks foreign investment to boost
nuclear sector - UPI.com\\n\\nTrending\\n\\nConan Harris\\n\\nMass shootings\\n\\nSoldier killed\\n\\nLettuce recall\\n\\nJens Spahn\\n\\n$500K lottery\\n\\nDog rescued\\n\\nSkydive
record\\n\\nJimothy raccoon\\n\\nMarch 11, 2026 / 12:51 PM\\n\\n\\u201cThe global nuclear renaissance is not a forecast. It is happening,\\u201d Federico Ramos, Argentina\\u2019s secretary for nuclear
affairs, told representatives from energy companies and other firms meeting in New York this week. .File Photo by CNEA/EPA\\n\\nBUENOS AIRES, M\", \"highlights\": [\"Argentina seeks foreign investment
to boost nuclear sector - UPI.com\\n...\\n\\u201cThe global nuclear renaissance is not a forecast. It is happening,\\u201d Federico Ramos, Argentina\\u2019s secretary for nuclear affairs, told
representatives from energy companies and other firms meeting in New York this week. .File Photo by CNEA/EPA\\n...\\nBUENOS AIRES, March 11 (UPI) -- Argentina's government presented investment and
cooperation opportunities in its nuclear industry to more than 50 U.S. companies this week, as officials seek to position the country as a partner in the global energy transition.\\n...\\nThe
presentation was made during Argentina Week 2026, held Monday through Wednesday in New York to bring together business leaders and multinational executives. A session titled \\\"Argentina's Nuclear
Sector: A New Stage of Development and Global Projection\\\" was held at the Argentine Consulate General.\\n...\\n\\\"The global nuclear renaissance is not a forecast. It is happening,\\\" Federico
Ramos, Argentina's secretary for nuclear affairs, told representatives from energy companies and other firms.\\n...\\nRamos said about 65 nuclear reactors are under construction worldwide, and that
woold is increase because of demand for uranium, nuclear fuel services and radioisotopes.\\n...\\n\\\"Argentina has the resources, the technology and now both the institutional framework and
macroeconomic stability to participate in that growth, not as a spectator, but as a partner,\\\" he said.\\n...\\nOfficials and technical experts outlined Argentina's capabilities across the nuclear
supply chain, including uranium mining, fuel production, technological development, specialized engineering and electricity generation.\\n...\\nRolando Granada, a physicist and researcher at
Argentina's National Atomic Energy Commission, told UPI that the government's goal is to attract foreign investment.\\n...\\n\\\"It would certainly be beneficial. The aim is to build partnerships and
align capabilities with investors, agencies or foreign companies that view nuclear power generation as a profitable business,\\\" Granada said.\\n...\\nHe added that while Argentina has technical
capacity, expansion requires financial resources the country currently lacks.\\n...\\n\\\"To continue growing and expanding, foreign investment is needed, since Argentina's financial capabilities in
this area are extremely limited,\\\" he said.\\n...\\nGranada also pointed to uranium as a sector with development potential. Argentina has uranium deposits used as nuclear fuel, but exploiting them
requires capital.\\n...\\n\\\"There are uranium deposits in Argentina. To develop them, investment is required,\\\" he said. However, he cautioned that known reserves are limited, meaning Argentina
would not be in a position to become a major uranium exporter.\\n...\\nThe United States relies heavily on nuclear energy and could face constraints in domestic uranium production within 15 years,
increasing its need for reliable foreign suppliers, he said.\\n...\\nGranada said promoting Argentina's nuclear sector abroad could benefit the country, but warned of trade-offs.\\n...\\n\\\"This
activity is positive for Argentina, but we have to consider that our export capacity is limited. If we export uranium, there may not be enough left for our own power plants,\\\" he
said.\\n...\\nArgentina's nuclear program has developed over roughly 75 years and has earned international recognition, he said. The country can design and build research reactors and has exported
that technology to other markets.\\n...\\nAmong current projects, Granada cited the CAREM small modular reactor, a fully Argentine-designed initiative that reflects the country's technological
capabilities and its effort to maintain a role in the global nuclear industry.\\n...\\n- Middle East crisis boosts energy opportunities for Argentina\\n- Argentine industrial groups break silence,

## Research Report: U.S.–Argentina Diplomatic Calendar, 19 Aug – 10 Sept 2026, and the Nuclear Cooperation Agreement

### Bottom line up front

**No bilateral summit, ministerial meeting, or announced signing ceremony is scheduled between the U.S. and Argentina in the 19 August – 10 September 2026 window.** Milei has no U.S. trip in this period; his next is UNGA (22–28 Sept). The IAEA General Conference — the obvious multilateral venue for a nuclear signing — falls on **14–18 September, four to eight days after the window closes**. Argentina's own stated target for signing the new nuclear agreement is "before the end of the year," not this window.

However, the relevant precedent (Paraguay, 4 Aug 2026) shows such signings do **not** require a summit: Secretary Rubio signed a civil nuclear MOU with Paraguay's foreign minister at the State Department on an ordinary working day. Argentine FM Quirno travels to Washington frequently and on short notice.

---

## 1. The nuclear agreement itself — status and mechanics

### What is actually pending
A **new Section 123 Agreement** (Agreement for Cooperation Concerning the Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy) to replace the existing one.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Current agreement signed | Buenos Aires, **29 February 1996** |
| Entered into force | **16 October 1997** |
| Term | 30 years |
| **Expires** | **16 October 2027** |
| Argentine ratification | Law 24.862 (sanctioned 13 Aug 1997, promulgated 10 Sept 1997) |

### Negotiation trajectory
- **18th JSCNEC** (Joint Standing Committee on Nuclear Energy Cooperation), Buenos Aires, 30 Sept – 3 Oct 2024: parties "committed to **commence** negotiations on the renewal."
- **19th JSCNEC**, Washington DC, **25–27 February 2026**: parties "reaffirmed their commitment to **swiftly complete** negotiations on the text of a new Agreement... to replace the current agreement, which expires in 2027." Co-chaired by **Gonzalo Suarez** (Deputy Assistant Secretary for Nonproliferation Policy, State/AVC) and **Federico Ramos Napoli** (Secretary of Nuclear Affairs, Argentine Ministry of Economy). U.S. delegation: State, DOE, NNSA, NRC, Commerce. Argentine: Cancillería/DIGAN, CNEA, ARN, Nucleoeléctrica, Embassy.
- **10 August 2026** (TN, Ignacio Salerno — syndicated across ~10 Argentine outlets): Casa Rosada says the **text is closed between technical teams**; Cancillería is "coordinating with Washington the steps to effect the signature during the coming months." Stated goal: **sign before end of 2026**.
- **No 20th JSCNEC meeting has been announced.**

### Post-signature requirement
After signature, a 123 Agreement requires **90 days of continuous session** congressional review in the U.S. before entry into force (absent a joint resolution of disapproval). Signing ≠ entry into force — an important distinction for any resolution language.

---

| Date | Event | In window? |
|---|---|---|
| ~9–18 Aug | Secluded at Quinta de Olivos (speech/book writing) | — |
| **20 Aug** | Council of the Americas, Buenos Aires | ✅ domestic |
| **21 Aug** | Bolsa de Comercio de Rosario | ✅ domestic |
| **22 Sept** | Departs for New York | ❌ after |
| **22/23–28 Sept** | UNGA 81 general debate | ❌ after |
| **29 Sept** | Paris (Argentina Week, 30 Sept – 2 Oct) | ❌ after |
| **13–14 Oct** | **Washington** — Official Hispanic Heritage Gala, Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium (19th U.S. trip; Trump expected to attend) | ❌ after |
| **14–15 Dec** | G20 Leaders' Summit, Miami (Trump National Doral; Trump hosts) | ❌ after |

FM **Pablo Quirno** accompanies Milei on all three trips. **No new Milei–Trump bilateral has been confirmed** for any of them.

---

## 3. IAEA General Conference 2026 — just misses the window

- **70th Regular Session: 14–18 September 2026**, Vienna International Centre.
- Confirmed by IAEA's own 2026 events preview and multiple independent listings.
- **Falls entirely outside 19 Aug – 10 Sept.** This is the single most likely natural venue for a nuclear-agreement signing or announcement, and it sits 4–8 days past the window boundary.

---

## 4. U.S. officials in Argentina during the window

There *is* high-level U.S. presence in Buenos Aires — but it is law-enforcement, not nuclear:

- **40th International Drug Enforcement Conference (IDEC)**, Palacio Libertad, Buenos Aires, **18–20 August 2026**. Opened by **DEA Administrator Terrence Cole** and Argentine Security Minister **Alejandra Monteoliva**. 400–1,000 delegates; closed to press. Cole met FM Quirno on the margins.
- **Cartwright Weiland**, Assistant Secretary of State for International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs — **on travel to Argentina 17–22 August 2026** (per State Dept public schedule, 18 Aug).
- **Ambassador Peter Lamelas** active in Buenos Aires: AmCham energy forum (~14–16 Aug), where he named **energy, mining, AI, and nuclear technology** as priority sectors; TN interview 15–16 Aug.

### Rubio's Argentina visit: postponed, no new date
- A standing invitation has existed since mid-2025 (extended to Energy Secretary Chris Wright in June 2025 and separately to Rubio).
- A Buenos Aires stop was called **"highly probable" for ~12 March 2026**, but was **shelved** amid Middle East escalation. Casa Rosada described it as a temporary postponement.
- As of August 2026, **no rescheduled date has been announced**.
- Context on contact frequency: by early March 2026, Quirno had reportedly held **seven direct conversations with Rubio** in that year alone — the relationship does not depend on summits.

---

## 5. The Paraguay precedent — how these get signed

**4 August 2026**: Secretary **Marco Rubio** and Paraguayan Foreign Minister **Rubén Ramírez Lezcano** signed a **Memorandum of Understanding for Strategic Civil Nuclear Cooperation (NCMOU)** at the Department of State. Low-key ceremony, remarks in English and Spanish, no summit.

Casa Rosada explicitly drew the distinction: an **NCMOU is not a 123 Agreement**. Paraguay had no prior framework; the NCMOU opens a partnership but does not authorize exports of nuclear material or equipment. Argentina has had a full 123 framework for nearly three decades, so its instrument is a *renewal/replacement*, legally heavier and congressionally reviewable.

This matters two ways: (a) it demonstrates a signing can occur at State on any working day; (b) it shows the administration is actively signing civil-nuclear instruments across Latin America right now.

---

## 6. Bilateral agreements already signed in 2026 (not available to "host" a signing)

- **4 Feb 2026** — Critical Minerals framework instrument. Signed by **Quirno + Deputy Secretary Christopher Landau** at the State Department, at the Rubio-hosted inaugural Critical Minerals Ministerial (Vance, Rubio, Bessent all spoke).
- **5 Feb 2026** — **ARTI** (U.S.–Argentina Agreement on Reciprocal Trade and Investment). Signed by **USTR Jamieson Greer + Quirno**, Washington. U.S. eliminates reciprocal tariffs on 1,675 Argentine products; Argentina scraps barriers on 200+ categories; Argentine beef quota quadrupled to 100,000 t/yr. Enters into force 60 days after exchange of notifications. Argentina was the first of four LatAm framework countries to finalize.

### Still pending (candidates for a future signing package)
- **Cybersecurity understanding** — under development since early 2026 (cooperation, technology, equipment, critical-infrastructure protection).
- **Space/satellite technical agreements** — Argentina already has an Artemis-related tie.
- The 10 Aug TN reporting bundles nuclear + cyber + space as one "strategic package" the government wants to deepen with Washington.

---

## 7. Argentine nuclear-sector context

- **July 2026**: Government unveiled **Meitner Energy** (U.S.-based) proposal — **USD 1.2 billion**, privately financed **ACR-300 SMR (~300 MWe)** at the **Atucha** site, INVAP design; ~2,000 direct jobs. Explicitly **independent of the 123 Agreement**, but illustrates the commercial pull.
- **2–4 June 2026**: 4th Annual **FIRST** (Foundational Infrastructure for Responsible Use of SMR Technology) Latin America & Caribbean regional workshop, **Buenos Aires**, co-hosted by U.S. and CNEA. Attended by Ambassador Lamelas and **Assistant Secretary Christopher Yeaw**. Argentina joined FIRST as a contributing partner in Sept 2025 — first Latin American country in that category.
- **3 June 2026**: "Guidelines for Argentine Nuclear Policy 2026" published; four priorities — high value-added exports, energy security, national technological capacity, regional leadership. Ramos Napoli: "reactivating uranium mining is a priority for this government."
- **10 June 2026**: Argentina–Chile nuclear cooperation agreement signed (CNEA–CCHEN).
- CAREM-25 SMR construction remains suspended at ~two-thirds complete.

---

## 8. Prediction markets

**No relevant markets found.** Searches across Polymarket, Manifold, and Kalshi returned nothing on U.S.–Argentina nuclear cooperation. No market-implied probability is available.

## 9. Data-vintage and reliability notes

- The "text is closed, awaiting diplomatic coordination" claim rests on **a single originating source** — TN's Ignacio Salerno, 10 Aug 2026, citing unnamed Casa Rosada officials — republished verbatim across many Argentine outlets. The syndication breadth should not be mistaken for independent corroboration.
- The official documentary record (State Dept / Cancillería joint statement, 5–6 Mar 2026) says only "swiftly complete negotiations," which is weaker than "text closed."
- Argentina's 2026 domestic calendar has **no national election** (midterms were Oct 2025; next general is 2027), so no domestic electoral constraint on signing in this window.
- Two named U.S. sources for the 123 expiry date (DOE/NNSA list and CRS RS22937, updated 10 Feb 2026) both give 16 October 2027, confirming the Argentine press reporting.

---

## 10. Summary answer to the question posed

Nothing in the 19 August – 10 September 2026 window is scheduled to host a nuclear cooperation agreement signing:

- No Milei trip to Washington, and none announced
- No announced Trump-administration cabinet-level visit to Buenos Aires (Rubio's remains indefinitely postponed)
- No announced Quirno trip to Washington
- No 20th JSCNEC meeting scheduled
- IAEA General Conference is 14–18 September — outside the window
- UNGA high-level week is 22–28 September — outside the window
- The one confirmed high-level bilateral event inside the window (IDEC, 18–20 Aug) is drug-enforcement, with no nuclear component

The nearest scheduled venues capable of hosting such a signing are, in order: **IAEA GC (14–18 Sept, Vienna)**, **UNGA (22–28 Sept, New York)**, and **Milei's Washington visit (13–14 Oct)** — the last of which sits two days before the 16 October anniversary of the current agreement's entry into force, one year out from its expiry.

## 💬 Response

Research complete. Key findings:

**The window is empty of hosting opportunities.** No bilateral summit, ministerial, or announced signing ceremony falls between 19 Aug and 10 Sept 2026. Milei's next foreign travel begins 22 September (UNGA); before that he has only domestic events (Council of the Americas 20 Aug, Rosario 21 Aug).

**The IAEA General Conference narrowly misses:** 14–18 September 2026, Vienna — 4 to 8 days after the window closes. This is the most natural multilateral venue for a nuclear signing and it sits just outside.

**The agreement itself is genuinely advanced but targeted later.** A replacement 123 Agreement is pending (current one expires 16 Oct 2027). The 19th JSCNEC (Washington, 25–27 Feb 2026) committed to "swiftly complete negotiations"; by 10 Aug 2026 Casa Rosada was saying the text is closed between technical teams with only diplomatic coordination remaining — but the stated target is **before end of 2026**, not this window. No 20th JSCNEC has been scheduled.

**Two findings that cut against a purely calendar-based read:**
1. The Paraguay precedent (4 Aug 2026) shows Rubio signing a civil nuclear MOU with a visiting foreign minister at the State Department on an ordinary working day — no summit required. Quirno travels to Washington frequently and on short notice.
2. There *is* senior U.S. presence in Buenos Aires inside the window — DEA Administrator Terrence Cole and State's Cartwright Weiland (17–22 Aug) for the 40th IDEC conference — but it is entirely law-enforcement, with no nuclear component.

**Two caveats worth carrying forward:** the "text is closed" claim traces to a single originating source (TN, 10 Aug) syndicated across many outlets, and is stronger than the official joint-statement language. And signing ≠ entry into force — a 123 Agreement then needs 90 days of continuous congressional session.

No prediction markets exist on this question across Polymarket, Manifold, or Kalshi.

One tooling note: AskNews returned 403s (tier-restricted to deepseek-basic / Spelunker+), so all research went through Exa, web search, and direct fetches. Agreements for Peaceful Cooperation | Department of Energy\", \"url\": \"https://www.energy.gov/nnsa/123-agreements-peaceful-cooperation\", \"snippet\": \"123 Agreements for Peaceful Cooperation |
Department of Energy\\n\\n# 123 Agreements for Peaceful Cooperation\\n\\nSection 123 of the U.S. Atomic Energy Act generally requires the conclusion of a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement for
significant transfers of nuclear material or equipment from the United States. Moreover, such agreements, commonly referred to as \\u201c123 Agreements,\\u201d facilitate cooperation in other areas,
such as technical exchanges, scientific research, and safeguards discussions. In c\", \"highlights\": [\"123 Agreements for Peaceful Cooperation | Department of Energy\\n\\n# 123 Agreements for
Peaceful Cooperation\\n\\nSection 123 of the U.S. Atomic Energy Act generally requires the conclusion of a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement for significant transfers of nuclear material or
equipment from the United States. Moreover, such agreements, commonly referred to as \\u201c123 Agreements,\\u201d facilitate cooperation in other areas, such as technical exchanges, scientific
research, and safeguards discussions. In conjunction with other nonproliferation tools, particularly the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), 123 Agreements help to advance U.S.
nonproliferation principles. These agreements establish the legal framework for significant nuclear cooperation with other countries. In order for a partner to enter into a 123 Agreement with the
United States, that partner must adhere to a set of strong nonproliferation requirements. The U.S. Department of State is responsible for negotiating 123 Agreements, with the technical assistance and
concurrence of DOE/NNSA and in consultation with the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission.\\n\\nAs of July 11, 2025, the United States has 26 such agreements in force that govern peaceful nuclear
cooperation with 50 countries, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the governing authorities on Taiwan (through the American Institute in Taiwan), as detailed below.\\n\\nUnited States
Agreements for Cooperation Partners (entry into force and expiration dates):\\n\\n- Argentina (16 October 1997/16 October 2027)\\n- Australia (22 December 2010/22 December 2040 with rolling 5-year
extensions)\\n- Brazil (15 September 1999/15 September 2029)\\n- Canada (21 July 1955/1 January 2030 with rolling 5-year extensions)\\n- China (29 October 2015/29 October 2045)\\n- European Atomic
Energy Community (Euratom)1 (12 April 1996/12 April 2026 with rolling 5-year extensions)\\n- International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) (7 August 1959/7 August 2054)\\n- India (6 December 2008/6
December 2048 with rolling 10-year extensions)\\n- Indonesia (30 December 1981/30 December 2031)\\n- Japan (17 July 1988/17 July 2018 but remains in force until terminated by a Party)\\n- Kazakhstan
(5 November 1999/5 November 2029)\\n- Republic of Korea (25 November 2015/25 November 2040)\\n- Mexico (2 November 2022/2 November 2052)\\n- Morocco (16 May 1981/16 May 2021 with rolling 5-year
extensions)\\n- Norway (19 January 2017/19 January 2047)\\n- Philippines (2 July 2024/2 July 2054)\\n- Russian Federation (11 January 2011/11 January 2041)\\n- Singapore (12 December 2024/12 December
2054)\\n- Switzerland (23 June 1998/23 June 2028 with rolling 5-year extensions)\\n- Taiwan2 (22 June 2014/indefinite)\\n- Thailand (9 July 2025/9 July 2055)\\n- Turkey (2 June 2008/2 June 2023 with
rolling 5-year extensions)\\n- Ukraine (28 May 1999/28 May 2029)\\n- United Arab Emirates (17 December 2009/17 December 2039)\\n- United Kingdom (31 December 2020/31 December 2050)\\n- Vietnam (3
October 2014/3 October 2044 with rolling 5-year extensions)\\n\\n1 Euratom comprises the following Member States: Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia,
Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, and Sweden.2 Pursuant to
Sections 4 and 6 of the Taiwan Relations Act, P.L. 96-8, 93 Stat. 14, and Executive Order 13014, 61 F.R. 42963, agreements relative to Taiwan shall be entered into, performed, and enforced, in the
manner and to the extent directed by the President, by or through the American Institute in Taiwan.\\n\\nThis page was last updated on July 11, 2025.\"], \"published_date\": null, \"score\": null},

\"snippet\": \"Civil Nuclear Cooperation Through 123 Agreements: A Primer | Lawfare\\n\\n---\\n\\nMeet The Authors\\n\\nSubscribe to Lawfare\\n\\nNews of Saudi Arabia\\u2019s alleged undeclared
nuclear cooperation with China to extract uranium yellowcake from uranium ore has generated bipartisan concern from U.S. lawmakers over the kingdom\\u2019s nuclear weapons intentions, and it may stoke
existing tensions between the White House and Congress over the administration\\u2019s lack of transparency over the United States\\u2019s own negotiations with\", \"highlights\": [\"for civil nuclear
cooperation. Since early 20\\n...\\nnuclear proliferation risks associated with concluding\\n...\\nnuclear cooperation agreement with\\n...\\nArabia could exploit reactor

force\\n...\\nA 123 agreement is a congressional-executive agreement that provides the overall legal framework for the United States to engage in civilian nuclear cooperation with a foreign country,
including the export of nuclear reactors, critical reactor components and reactor fuel.\\n...\\nIf in concluding a 123 agreement, the president has secured all required guarantees from the cooperating
country, then the agreement functions as an ex ante congressional-executive agreement, meaning that the agreement will enter into force without any required action from Congress. Specifically, the
statute describes a requirement for 90 days of continuous session after which the agreement enters into force absent a joint resolution disapproving of the agreement.\\n...\\nIf, however, the
president has exempted a country from any of the requirements specifically provided under the Atomic Energy Act, then the agreement can better be understood as an ex post congressional-executive
agreement, whereby Congress must approve, by joint resolution, any such 123 agreement for it to enter into force.\\n...\\nFurthermore, Section 123 ensures that Congress stays in the loop as these
agreements are being negotiated to an unusual degree. The president is required by statute to keep the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the Senate Foreign Relations Committee \\u201cfully and
currently informed of any initiative or negotiations relating to a new or amended\\u201d civil nuclear cooperation agreement.\\n...\\nThis bipartisan slate of senators and members of
Congress\\u2014including Sens. Rubio and Markey and Reps. Sherman and Yoho\\u2014have introduced various bills that would grant Congress greater oversight and control over both newly minted 123
agreements and any that would be up for renewal. The latest of such proposals is the Preventing the Spread of Nuclear Weapons Act of 2019, which is currently in committee review in both the House and
Senate and was preceded by the Saudi Nuclear Nonproliferation Act of 2019 and the Preventing Nuclear Proliferation in Saudi Arabia Act of 2019.\\n...\\nMost critically, the bill has the potential to
flip the existing standard for congressional passage of 123 agreements on its head. If the cooperating nation has shown any propensity to garner secret nuclear weapons ambitions, the bill would
require Congress to pass a joint resolution affirmatively approving of the agreement for it to enter into force. More specifically, the proposed statute would require that the president\\u2014at the
time of submitting a 123 agreement to Congress\\u2014also submit a report detailing \\u201cany credible evidence\\u201d that the cooperating country intends to \\u201cpursue a nuclear program that is
not inherently peaceful\\u201d and citing any instance in which the country has \\u201cviolated international standards with respect to the development, storage, deployment or use\\u201d of weapons of
mass destruction. If either of these reporting requirements is triggered, then Congress must approve the 123 agreement by joint resolution for it to be enacted.\\n...\\npast decade in amending the

Association\\n\\nFact Sheets & Briefs\\n\\nLast Reviewed\\n\\nSeptember 2023\\n\\nContacts: Kelsey Davenport, Director for Nonproliferation Policy, (202)-463-8270 ext. 102; Daryl Kimball, Executive
Director, (202) 463-8270 x107;\\n\\nSection 123 of the U.S. Atomic Energy Act (AEA) of 1954 establishes the conditions and outlines the process for major nuclear cooperation between the United States
and other countries. In order for a country to enter int\", \"highlights\": [\"Section 123 requires that the Department of State submit a Nuclear Proliferation Assessment Statement (NPAS) explaining
how the nuclear cooperation agreement meets these nonproliferation conditions. Congress has a total of 90 days in continuous session to consider the agreement, after which it automatically becomes law
unless Congress adopts a joint resolution opposing it.\\n...\\nThe President may exempt a proposed agreement from any of the above criteria upon determination maintaining such a criteria would be
\\u201cseriously prejudicial to the achievement of U.S. non-proliferation objectives or otherwise jeopardize the common defense of the United States.\\u201d Exempted 123 agreements would then go
through a different process than non-exempt agreements, requiring a congressional joint resolution approving the agreement for it to become law. There are no 123 agreements in force that were adopted
with such exemptions.\\n...\\nIn 2006, Congress passed the Henry J. Hyde United States-India Peaceful Atomic Energy Cooperation Act which amended the AEA to permit nuclear cooperation with India, a
country which is not a member of the nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty (NPT) and does not maintain full-scope safeguards. The Hyde amendment has been criticized for undermining U.S. and international
counterproliferation efforts, including the Nuclear Suppliers Group. The 40-year U.S.-India 123 agreement came into force in December 2008.\\n...\\nThe Trump administration submitted signed new 123
agreements with Mexico and the United Kingdom to Congress in May 2018. The United Kingdom was previously covered under the U.S.-European Atomic Energy Community (EURATOM) 123 agreement, but after the
UK withdraws from the European Union, the bilateral agreement between the U.S. and the EU will take effect. Japan\\u2019s agreement technically expired in 2018, but renewal terms dictate that the
agreement shall remain in force until terminated by a party.\\n...\\nThe next agreement that will expire without renewal terms in place (which could trigger an easier automatic renewal without the
need to renegotiate or resubmit the agreement to Congress) will be with Egypt in December 2021.\"], \"published_date\": null, \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"Nuclear Cooperation with Other

Countries:\\n\\n### A Primer\\n\\nIn order for the United States to engage in significant civilian nuclear cooperation with other states, it must conclude a framework agreement that meets specific
requirements under Section 123 of the Atomic Energy Act (AEA). Signi\", \"highlights\": [\"In order for the United States to engage in significant civilian nuclear cooperation with other states, it
must conclude a framework agreement that meets specific requirements under Section 123 of the Atomic Energy Act (AEA). Significant nuclear cooperation includes the export of reactors, critical parts
of reactors, and reactor fuel. The AEA also provides for export control licensing procedures and criteria for terminating cooperation. Congressional review is required for Section 123 agreements; the
AEA establishes special parliamentary procedures by which Congress may act on a proposed agreement.\\n...\\nSuch agreements, which are \\u201ccongressional-executive agreements\\n...\\nrequiring
congressional review\\n...\\nreference and authorize cooperation\\n...\\ncooperation will take place\\n...\\nrequirements for an agreement\\n...\\ncontent, conditions for the\\n...\\nto exempt an
agreement from those requirements, presidential determinations and\\n...\\n, conditions affecting the implementation of an agreement once it takes effect\\n...\\n#### Congressional
Review\\n...\\nUnder the AEA, Congress has the opportunity to review a nuclear cooperation agreement for two time periods totaling 90 days of continuous session. 9 The President must submit the text
of the proposed agreement, along with required supporting documents (including the unclassified NPAS) to the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. The President
is to consult with the committees \\u201cfor a period of not less than 30 days of continuous session.\\u201d After this period of consultation, the President is to submit the agreement to Congress,
along with the classified annex to the NPAS and a statement of the President\\u2019s approval of the agreement and determination that it will not damage U.S. national security interests. This action
begins the second period, which consists of 60 days of continuous session. In practice, the President has sent the agreement to Congress at the beginning of the full 90-day period, which begins on the
date of transmittal. Typically, the 60-day period has immediately followed the expiration of the 30-day period. The President transmits the text of the proposed agreement along with a letter of
support with a national security determination, the unclassified NPAS, its classified annex, and letters of support for the agreement from the Secretary of State and the Nuclear Regulatory
Commission.\\n...\\nIf the President has not exempted the agreement from any Section 123a requirements, the \\nagreement may enter into force after the end of the 60-day period unless, during that
time, \\nCongress adopts a joint resolution disapproving the agreement and the resolution becomes law. In \\norder for an exempted agreement to enter into force, Congress must adopt a joint resolution
of \\napproval and it must become law by the end of the 60-day period. At the beginning of this 60-day \\nperiod, joint resolutions of approval or disapproval, as appropriate, are to be automatically
\\nintroduced in each house. During this period, the committees are to hold hearings on the proposed \\nagreement and \\u201csubmit a report to their respective bodies recommending whether it should
be \\napproved or disapproved.\\u201d If either committee has not reported the requisite joint resolution of \\napproval or disapproval by the end of 45 days, the resolution is automatically
discharged from \\nfurther consideration of the measure. After the joint resolution is reported or discharged, Congress \\nis to consider it under expedited procedures, as established by Section
130.i. of the AEA. \\nCongress has used procedures outside the above-described process to adopt legislation approving \\nsome nuclear cooperation agreements (see Appendix C).\\n...\\nof P.\\n...\\n.

Tiananmen\\n...\\nThis CRS Report discusses renewal of the peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement between the United States and the People\\u2019s Republic of China (PRC). The current agreement was
signed in 1985 and implemented in 1998. The agreement is set to expire on December 30, 2015, and a new agreement was submitted for congressional review on April 21, 2015. 1 The required congressional
review period ended on July 31, 2015, and the agreement may enter into force. The discussion in this report focuses on congressional roles in crafting and carrying out the agreement. Such agreements
are subject to Section 123 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 as amended (AEA, P.L. 95-242, 42 U.S.C. 2011 et seq.) and commonly are called \\u201c123 agreements.\\u201d 2 They are a prerequisite for
any significant nuclear cooperation 3 with another country, such as exports of nuclear power plants and components and the transfer of nuclear material. 4\\n...\\nThe Obama Administration has
submitted the new U.S.-China nuclear cooperation agreement to Congress for the required review period. According to President Obama\\u2019s letter to Congress, the agreement meets all the terms of the
Atomic Energy Act 5 and does not require any exemptions from the law\\u2019s requirements. Therefore, the agreement could enter into force after a 30-day consultation period and a review period of 60
days of continuous session 6 unless Congress enacted a joint resolution of disapproval. Congress also has the option of adopting either a joint resolution of approval with (or without) conditions, or
stand-alone legislation that could approve or disapprove the agreement. Any congressional efforts to block the agreement would be subject to presidential veto. The agreement reached the end of the
review period on July 31.\\n...\\nIn a Senate\\n...\\nhearing held on May 12, Chairman Bob Corker said that \\u201cthere may be a series of conditions that the Senate may want to place on this
particular agreement\\u201d and that the members of the committee would be considering the merits of that option. Two pieces of legislation have been introduced regarding this agreement. House Joint
Resolution 56 (H.J.Res. 56), introduced in May by Representative Joe Wilson and co-sponsored by Representative Brendan Boyle, would have approved the U.S.-China Section 123 agreement. Senators Marco
Rubio and Tom Cotton introduced S.J.Res. 19 on July 15, which expressed \\u201cdisfavor\\u201d of the proposed agreement. This resolution was automatically discharged from the Senate Foreign Relations
Committee and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Since no action was taken before the congressional review period for this agreement ended on July 31, the agreement may
enter into force.\\n...\\nsigned the agreement on July 2\\n...\\n, 1\\n...\\n. On July\\n...\\n, 198\\n...\\n, President Reagan submitted the agreement to Congress. Consideration of whether a
presidential certification (as required by P.L. 99-183 on China\\u2019s nuclear nonproliferation policy and practices) would be the centerpiece of a summit in 1997 advanced the agreement\\u2019s
implementation. President Clinton, on January 12, 1998, signed certifications to implement the agreement. The President also waived a sanction imposed after the 1989 Tiananmen Crackdown (in P.L.
101-246). Congressional review ended on March 18, 1998, allowing the agreement to be implemented. Almost 13 years passed between the time that President Reagan submitted the agreement to Congress in
July 1985 and its implementation in March 1998 under the Clinton Administration. Congress played an important role in determining implementation of the agreement, including holding hearings, crafting
legislation, and requiring and reviewing presidential certifications. One of the primary congressional actions was P.L. 99-183, the Joint Resolution Relating to the Approval and Implementation of the
Proposed Agreement for Nuclear Cooperation Between the United States and the People\\u2019s Republic of China (December 16, 1985), which required a presidential certification and a report followed by
a period of 30 days of continuous session of Congress before the agreement could be implemented. After the 1989 Tiananmen Crackdown, Congress enacted sanctions in P.L. 101-246, the Foreign Relations

Nuclear Cooperation Agreements\", \"url\": \"https://armscontrolcenter.org/civil-nuclear-cooperation-agreements/\", \"snippet\": \"Fact Sheet: Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreements - Center for Arms
Control and Non-Proliferation\\n\\n- Skip to main content\\n- Skip to primary sidebar\\n- Skip to footer\\n\\nUpdated March 2021\\n\\nUnder Section 123 of the U.S. Atomic Energy Act, the United States
cannot make any significant transfers of nuclear material, equipment, or components to another nation without a congressionally-approved agreement. The United States has so-called \\u201c123
agreements\\u201d with 24 countries, and is currently engaged in form\", \"highlights\": [\"Fact Sheet: Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreements - Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation\\n\\n- Skip
to main content\\n- Skip to primary sidebar\\n- Skip to footer\\n\\nUpdated March 2021\\n\\nUnder Section 123 of the U.S. Atomic Energy Act, the United States cannot make any significant transfers of
nuclear material, equipment, or components to another nation without a congressionally-approved agreement. The United States has so-called \\u201c123 agreements\\u201d with 24 countries, and is
currently engaged in formal negotiations for a nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia.\\n\\nCertain materials, equipment, and components used for civil nuclear energy programs can also be
used for nuclear weapons programs. In order to reduce those risks, countries seeking a 123 agreement with the United States must commit to nine nonproliferation criteria. These criteria require the
partner country to obtain U.S. consent before taking certain actions, including any enrichment or reprocessing of nuclear material obtained or produced as a result of the agreement. However, the
required nonproliferation conditions for a 123 agreement do not prohibit the partner country from engaging in enrichment and reprocessing, provided that none of the nuclear material or facilities
involved were acquired, produced, or constructed as a result of the 123 agreement.\\n\\nThe Department of State leads the 123 agreement process by submitting to Congress a Nuclear Proliferation
Assessment Statement, which explains how the particular proposed agreement will meet these required nonproliferation criteria.\\n\\n## The Gold Standard\\n\\nTechnologies used to enrich and reprocess
nuclear fuel can also be used to produce material for nuclear weapons, and so present the greatest threat for proliferation. As part of its 123 agreement, the United Arab Emirates agreed not to seek
enrichment and reprocessing technologies and to instead rely on the international market for its reactor fuel supply. That commitment, in combination with the nonproliferation criteria required for
all 123 agreements, has come to be known as the nonproliferation \\u201cGold Standard\\u201d for civil nuclear cooperation agreements.\\n\\n## Congressional Approval Process for 123
Agreements\\n\\nAfter the Department of State submits a proposed 123 agreement to Congress, current U.S. law allows Congress to review the agreement for 90 days of continuous session. If Congress does
not pass a resolution disapproving of the agreement during this period, the agreement may enter into force. In recent years, nonproliferation experts have recommended that Congressional oversight be
strengthened over nuclear cooperation agreements to better protect against nuclear proliferation.\\n\\nOne idea under consideration is a bipartisan proposal introduced in the House of Representatives
on March 21, 2018 that seeks to ensure that any partner country entering into a 123 agreement with the United States should renounce the pursuit of enrichment and reprocessing facilities. Under the
bill, proposed 123 agreements that do not include the \\u201cGold Standard\\u201d of renouncing domestic enrichment and reprocessing capabilities would face a stronger Congressional approval process,
including an affirmative vote.\"], \"published_date\": \"2018-04-24T00:00:00.000\", \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"U.S. Nuclear Cooperation as Nonproliferation: Reforms, or the ...\", \"url\":
\"https://www.nti.org/analysis/articles/us-nuclear-cooperation-nonproliferation-reforms-or-devil-you-know/\", \"snippet\": \"U.S. Nuclear Cooperation as Nonproliferation: Reforms, or the Devil You
Know?\\n\\nClose\\n\\nReport Nov 26, 2012\\n\\n# U.S. Nuclear Cooperation as Nonproliferation: Reforms, or the Devil You Know?\\n\\nU.S. Nuclear Cooperation as Nonproliferation: Reforms, or the Devil
You Know?\\n\\n##### Jessica C. Varnum\\n\\nSenior Research Associate, The James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies\\n\\nThe United States and South Korea recently postponed further
negotiation of a controversial bilateral nuclear trade agreement s\", \"highlights\": [\"Unlike treaties, which require Senate approval, 123 agreements are congressional-executive agreements. Under
the Atomic Energy Act Congress can only prevent entry-into-force of a non-exempt agreement if both houses pass a resolution disapproving it. (However, so-called \\\"exempt\\\" agreements, in which the
prospective partner fails to meet one or more of Section 123a's nonproliferation requirements, require a joint resolution of congressional approval.) Following an executive-legislative
\\\"consultation\\\" period of 30 days of continuous session, non-exempt agreements must sit before Congress for 60 days of continuous session; unless Congress enacts a joint resolution of disapproval
during this period, the agreement automatically enters into force.[10]\\n...\\nquestionable export controls\\u2014a situation that would be worsened by subsequent\\n...\\nin the activities
of\\n...\\n] As such, the\\n...\\nEntry into force The\\n...\\nall provisions of\\n...\\nbinding on its parties. Every treaty specifies preconditions for its entry into force. For example, the NPT
specified that it would enter into force after the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Soviet Union (the Depository governments) and 40 other countries ratified the treaty, an event that
occurred on March 5, 1970. See entries for Signature, Ratification.\"], \"published_date\": \"2012-11-26T00:00:00.000\", \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"Prospects for U.S.-Saudi Nuclear Energy
Cooperation\", \"url\": \"https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IF/PDF/IF10799/IF10799.28.pdf\", \"snippet\": \"https://crsreports.congress.gov\\n\\nUpdated May 26, 2026\\n\\n## Prospects for

explains the agreement\\u2019s compliance with nonproliferation requirements.\\n\\nCongress then reviews the 123 Agreement. Although the AEA contemplates a 30-day consultation period before the

not act, the 123 Agreement takes effect after 90 days of \\u201ccontinuous session.\\u201d If Congress wants to prevent an agreement from taking effect, it must pass a joint resolution of disapproval
before the end of the 90-day period.\\n\\nPotential for Nuclear Power in Thailand\\n\\nThe United States and Thailand entered into a 123 Agreement in 1974, but this agreement expired in 2014. During

Vietnam on the Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy\\n\\nMay 08, 2014\\n\\nTo the Congress of the United States:\", \"highlights\": [\"# Message to the Congress Transmitting the Agreement for Cooperation
Between the United States and Vietnam on the Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy\\n...\\nMay 08, 2014\\n...\\nI am pleased to transmit to the Congress, pursuant to sections 123 b. and 123 d. of the Atomic
Energy Act of 1954, as amended (42 U.S.C. 2153(b), (d)) (the \\\"Act\\\"), the text of a proposed Agreement for Cooperation between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of
the Socialist Republic of Vietnam Concerning Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy (the \\\"Agreement\\\"). I am also pleased to transmit my written approval, authorization, and determination concerning the
Agreement, and an unclassified Nuclear Proliferation Assessment Statement (NPAS) concerning the Agreement. (In accordance with section 123 of the Act, as amended by title XII of the Foreign Affairs
Reform and Restructuring Act of 1998 (Public Law 105-277), a classified annex to the NPAS, prepared by the Secretary of State in consultation with the Director of National Intelligence, summarizing
relevant classified information, will be submitted to the Congress separately.) The joint memorandum submitted to me by the Secretaries of State and Energy and a letter from the Chairman of the
Nuclear Regulatory Commission stating the views of the Commission are also enclosed. An addendum to the NPAS containing a comprehensive analysis of Vietnam's export control system with respect to
nuclear-related matters, including interactions with other countries of proliferation concern and the actual or suspected nuclear, dual-use, or missile-related transfers to such countries, pursuant to
section 102A of the National Security Act of 1947 (50 U.S.C. 403-1), as amended, is being submitted separately by the Director of National Intelligence.\\n...\\nThe proposed Agreement has been
negotiated in accordance with the Act and other applicable law. In my judgment, it meets all applicable statutory requirements and will advance the nonproliferation and other foreign policy interests
of the United States.\\n...\\nThe proposed Agreement provides a comprehensive framework for peaceful nuclear cooperation with Vietnam based on a mutual commitment to nuclear nonproliferation. Vietnam
has affirmed that it does not intend to seek to acquire sensitive fuel cycle capabilities, but instead will rely upon the international market in order to ensure a reliable nuclear fuel supply for
Vietnam. This political commitment by Vietnam has been reaffirmed in the preamble of the proposed Agreement. The Agreement also contains a legally binding provision that prohibits Vietnam from
enriching or reprocessing U.S.-origin material without U.S. consent.\\n...\\nThe proposed Agreement will have an initial term of 30 years from the date of its entry into force, and will continue in
force thereafter for additional periods of 5 years each. Either party may terminate the Agreement on 6 months' advance written notice at the end of the initial 30 year term or at the end of any
subsequent 5-year period. Additionally, either party may terminate the Agreement on 1 year's written notice. I recognize the importance of executive branch consultations with the Congress regarding
the status of the Agreement prior to the end of the 30-year period after entry into force and prior to the end of each 5-year period thereafter. To that end, it is my strong recommendation that future
administrations conduct such consultations with the appropriate congressional committees at the appropriate times.\\n...\\nI have considered the views and recommendations of the interested departments
and agencies in reviewing the proposed Agreement and have determined that its performance will promote, and will not constitute an unreasonable risk to, the common defense and security. Accordingly, I
have approved the Agreement and authorized its execution and urge that the Congress give it favorable consideration.\\n...\\nThis transmission shall constitute a submittal for purposes of both
sections 123 b. and 123 d. of the Act. My Administration is prepared to begin immediately the consultations with the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee as
provided for in section 123 b. Upon completion of the 30 days of continuous session review provided for in section 123 b., the 60 days of continuous session review provided for in section 123 d. shall
commence.\\n...\\nMay 8, 2014.\"], \"published_date\": \"2014-05-08T00:00:00.000\", \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"Presidential Documents\", \"url\":

with an unclassified Nuclear Proliferation Assessment Statement (NPAS), which the President is to submit, along with the agreement, to those two committees. The State Department is also required to
provide a classified annex to the NPAS, prepared in consultation with the Director of National Intelligence. The NPAS is meant to explain the agreement\\u2019s compliance with the AEA nonproliferation
requirements. The President must also make a written determination \\u201cthat the performance of the proposed agreement will promote and will not constitute an unreasonable risk to, the common
defense and security.\\u201d In the case of a government that is not implementing an Additional Protocol to the government\\u2019s IAEA safeguards agreement, Section 1264 of the National Defense
Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2020 (P.L. 116-92) prohibits the President from providing to Congress an NPAS for a nuclear cooperation agreement. 5 This requirement is waived \\u201c90 days after
the date on which the President submits\\u201d to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and the House and Senate Armed Services Committees \\u201ca report
describing the manner in which such agreement would advance the national security and defense interests of the United States and not contribute to the proliferation of nuclear
weapons.\\u201d\\n...\\nUnder the AEA, Congress has the opportunity to review a nuclear cooperation agreement for two \\ntime periods totaling 90 days of continuous session. 10 The President must
submit the text of the \\nproposed agreement, along with required supporting documents (including the unclassified \\nNPAS) to the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the Senate Foreign Relations
Committee. \\nThe President is to consult with the committees \\u201cfor a period of not less than\\u201d 30 days of \\ncontinuous session. After this period of consultation, the President is to
submit the agreement to \\nCongress, along with the classified annex to the NPAS and a statement of the President\\u2019s approval \\nof the agreement and determination that it will not damage U.S.
national security interests. This \\naction begins the second period, which consists of 60 days of continuous session. In practice, the \\nPresident has sent the agreement to Congress at the beginning
of the full 90-day period, which\\n...\\nbegins on the date of transmittal. Typically, the 60-day period has immediately followed the \\nexpiration of the 30-day period. The President transmits the
text of the proposed agreement along\\n...\\nwith a letter of support with a national security determination, the unclassified NPAS, its \\nclassified annex, and letters of support for the agreement
from the Secretary of State and the \\nNuclear Regulatory Commission. \\nIf the President has not exempted the agreement from any Section 123a requirements, the \\nagreement may enter into force after
the end of the 60-day period unless, during that time, \\nCongress adopts a joint resolution disapproving the agreement and the resolution becomes law. In \\norder for an exempted agreement to enter
into force, Congress must adopt a joint resolution of \\napproval and it must become law by the end of the 60-day period. At the beginning of this 60-day \\nperiod, joint resolutions of approval or
disapproval, as appropriate, are to be automatically \\nintroduced in each house. During this period, the committees are to hold hearings on the proposed \\nagreement and \\u201csubmit a report to
their respective bodies recommending whether it should be \\napproved or disapproved.\\u201d If either committee has not reported the requisite joint resolution of \\napproval or disapproval by the
end of 45 days, the resolution is automatically discharged from \\nfurther consideration of the measure. After the joint resolution is reported or discharged, Congress \\nis to consider it under
expedited procedures, as established by Section 130.i. of the AEA. \\nCongress has used procedures outside the above-described process to adopt legislation approving \\nsome nuclear cooperation
agreements (see Appendix C).\\n...\\nA proposed subsequent arrangement shall not take effect before\\n...\\n5 days after publication\\n...\\ndetermination and notice\\n...\\nState is required to

\"highlights\": [\"# Message to the Congress Transmitting a Proposed Agreement for Cooperation Between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the United Mexican States
Concerning Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy\\n...\\nMay 08, 2018\\n...\\nTo the Congress of the United States:\\n...\\nI am pleased to transmit to the Congress, pursuant to subsections 123 b. and 123
d. of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended (42 U.S.C. 2153(b), (d)) (the \\\"Act\\\"), the text of an Agreement between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the
United Mexican States for Cooperation in Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy (the \\\"Agreement\\\"). I am also pleased to transmit my written approval, authorization, and determination concerning the
Agreement and an unclassified Nuclear Proliferation Assessment Statement (NPAS) concerning the Agreement. In accordance with section 123 of the Act, a classified annex to the NPAS, prepared by the
Secretary of State, in consultation with the Director of National Intelligence, summarizing relevant classified information, will be submitted to the Congress separately. A joint memorandum submitted
to me by the Secretaries of State and Energy and a letter from the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission stating the views of the Commission are also enclosed. An addendum to the NPAS
containing a comprehensive analysis of the export control system of Mexico with respect to nuclear-related matters, including interactions with other countries of proliferation concern and the actual
or suspected nuclear, dual-use, or missile-related transfers to such countries, pursuant to section 102A(w) of the National Security Act of 1947 (50 U.S.C. 3024(w)), is being submitted separately by
the Director of National Intelligence.\\n...\\nThe Agreement has been negotiated in accordance with the Act and other applicable law. In my judgment, it meets all applicable statutory requirements and
will advance the nonproliferation and other foreign policy interests of the United States.\\n...\\nThe Agreement has a term of 30 years, although it can be terminated by either party on one year's
advance written notice. In the event of termination or expiration of the Agreement, key nonproliferation conditions and controls will continue in effect as long as any material, equipment, or
component subject to the Agreement remains in the territory of the party concerned or under its jurisdiction or control anywhere, or until such time as the parties agree that such material, equipment,
or components are no longer usable for any nuclear activity relevant from the point of view of safeguards.\\n...\\nI have considered the views and recommendations of the interested departments and
agencies in reviewing the Agreement and have determined that its performance will promote, and will not constitute an unreasonable risk to, the common defense and security. Accordingly, I have
approved the Agreement and authorized its execution and urge that the Congress give it favorable consideration.\\n...\\nThis transmission shall constitute a submittal for purposes of both subsections
123 b. and 123 d. of the Act. My Administration is prepared to begin immediately consultations with the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee, as provided in
subsection 123 b. Upon completion of the 30 days of continuous session review provided for in subsection 123 b., the 60 days of continuous session review provided for in subsection 123 d. shall
commence.\\n...\\nMay 8, 2018.\\n...\\nMessage to the Congress Transmitting a Proposed Agreement for Cooperation Between the Government of the United States of America and\\n...\\nUnited Mexican

\"highlights\": [\"Armenia has less than a decade to decide who will build the nuclear power plant that is expected to replace the Soviet-era Metsamor facility after its planned decommissioning in

only one of its two comparatively small VVER-440 reactors, still accounting for as much as 30% of Armenia\\u2019s energy generation. Both of the plant's units were shut down following Armenia\\u2019s

megawatts in nuclear power generation to upwards of 1000.\\n...\\nOfficially, Yerevan is also considering China, France, South Korea and the United States for its next NPP partnership. Speaking in
February 2026, Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure Davit Khudatyan said officials were reviewing proposals from roughly a dozen companies.\\n...\\nWhen U.S. Vice President JD

providing future reactors.\\n...\\nFor Yerevan\\u2019s nuclear power ambitions, there are more than simply political considerations. Armenian officials have articulated their preference that

the world.\\n...\\nMeanwhile, though the agreement between the United States and Armenia explicitly referred to SMRs, there is no U.S. nuclear energy firm currently engaged in SMR NPP construction.

acquiring a SMR reactor from a U.S. firm, especially from a new generation of growing start-ups looking to build SMRs.\\n...\\nCamacho likewise pointed to the Bill Gates-backed TerraPower as a

\"highlights\": [\"29 Jul 2026 | Insights, Politics, Armenia \\n\\nAs Armenia prepares for a new era in energy policy, the country is once again turning to nuclear power \\u2014 but with a very
