nuclear plants designed to be safer, faster to build, and more adaptable to the needs of smaller countries. Armenia is currently working to prolong the operation of the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant by
an additional decade, until 2036, when it intends to replace it with a small modular reactor-based facility.\\n...\\nFor Armenia, a nation seeking greater energy independence while balancing economic
and geopolitical pressures, the shift toward modular nuclear technology could mark one of the most consequential infrastructure decisions since the construction of the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant.
Yet the plans have already sparked debate, with critics questioning the financial viability, long-term safety, and geopolitical implications of adopting relatively untested nuclear technologies.
Although Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan insists that the construction of a new nuclear power plant in Armenia is an economic rather than a political issue, the choice of foreign partner \\u2014
whether Russia, the United States, France, China, or South Korea \\u2014 is widely seen as a decision that could shape the country\\u2019s geopolitical orientation for decades. Experts from American
energy consulting firms recently visited Armenia to support the country\\u2019s assessment of U.S. small modular reactor technology following a pre-feasibility study on replacing the Metsamor nuclear
power plant. Russia has proposed to Armenia a high-capacity nuclear power plant project that could meet the country\\u2019s energy needs for decades, if not a century, according to a Russian Foreign
Ministry official in an interview with TASS. As of now, Armenian authorities have not made a final decision on which country they will cooperate with to build a new nuclear power plant meaning the
choice of technology and partner remains open. Meanwhile, Armenian experts are currently assessing the most suitable option for the country\\u2019s future nuclear energy strategy, including a detailed
evaluation of the advantages and disadvantages of small modular reactor technology.\\n...\\nAra Marjanyan\\n...\\nkey drawback of small modular nuclear reactors is\\n...\\nthey are not yet in

designs. There are less developed proposals from South Korea and France. With the United States, a process is underway under the so-called \\u201cOne-Two-Three\\u201d agreement framework, which has

Linkedin\\n- Share on Facebook\\n\\n(Image credit: US Embassy Yerevan via X)\\n\\nExperts from the American company Sargent & Lundy visited Yerevan as part of the US State Department\\u2019s
Fundamental Infrastructure for the Responsible Use of Small Modular Reactor Technology (FIRST) programme. The US Embassy in Armenia, said Sargent & Lundy in cooperation with Armenian officials, had
completed a prelimina\", \"highlights\": [\"US offers SMRs to Armenia - Nuclear Engineering International\\n...\\nExperts from the American company Sargent & Lundy visited Yerevan as part of the US
State Department\\u2019s Fundamental Infrastructure for the Responsible Use of Small Modular Reactor Technology (FIRST) programme. The US Embassy in Armenia, said Sargent & Lundy in cooperation with
Armenian officials, had completed a preliminary feasibility study to assess the possibility of replacing the Armenian Nuclear Power Plant (NPP) with new American technologies for small modular
reactors (SMRs).\\n...\\n\\u201cThe US Embassy in Yerevan welcomes further progress in cooperation between the US and Armenia in the field of civil nuclear energy,\\u201d the US Embassy said in a
Facebook post. It is also noted that based on the results, four of the most suitable American technologies for SMRs were identified for operation in Armenia. It said technical assistance was aligned
with International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) best practices, focusing on the highest standards of nuclear safety, security and non-proliferation and considering options for the development of
replacement capacity following the decommissioning of the Armenian NPP (ANPP).\\n...\\nThe four leading US small modular reactor (SMR) technologies identified for the potential replacement of the
Armenian Nuclear Power Plant\\u2019s power unit include the NuScale Power Module, GE Hitachi\\u2019s BWRX-300, Westinghouse\\u2019s AP300 SMR, and X-energy\\u2019s Xe-100, as supported by Sargent &
Lundy\\u2019s SMR portfolio analysis. These technologies represent the core of the US State Department\\u2019s civil nuclear framework, focusing on modular designs suitable for integration into
Armenia\\u2019s power grid.\\n...\\nThe ANPP at Metsamor was built in the 1970s with two Soviet-supplied VVER-440-V230 units but was closed following a devastating earthquake in 1988. However, unit 2
was recommissioned with Russian help in 1995 following severe energy shortages. In March 2014, the Armenian government decided to extend the plant\\u2019s service life to 2026.\\n...\\nMost of the
overhaul (until 2019) was funded by an interstate loan from Russia. In December 2024, following a meeting of the Armenian-Russian intergovernmental commission it was decided to extend the life of the
plant until 2036. The Armenian government allocated $65m for the implementation of the programme, which is being undertaken by Russian company Rusatom Service.\\n...\\nConstruction of a new nuclear
plant has long been part of Armenia\\u2019s overall plan, although finance has proved to be an obstacle. In 2024, Pashinyan said it was planning to build a new NPP within 8-10 years, and a preliminary
feasibility study for the construction of a new 1200 MWe unit was under consideration. At that time, Gera Sevikyan, Advisor to the ANPP Director General told ArmInfo that a fundamental decision had
been made to build a new unit using the Russian TOI reactor with a capacity of 1,200 MWe.\\n...\\nHowever intense lobbying by the US has since changed the perspective. In February, Armenia and the US
signed a bilateral civil nuclear cooperation agreement (a 123 Agreement), and the US pledged a $9bn investment in Armenia\\u2019s nuclear energy sector. This includes $5bn in upfront technology
exports and $4bn for long-term fuel and maintenance contracts.\\n...\\nArmenia continues to weigh the American SMR proposal alongside modular offers from Russia, South Korea, France, and China.
Earlier in May, the director of the fourth department of the CIS countries of the Russian Foreign Ministry, Mikhail Kalugin, said in an interview with TASS that Russia had proposed to Armenia a
nuclear power plant project that could meet the needs of the republic \\u201cfor a century to come\\u201d.\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-05-27T00:00:00.000\", \"score\": null}, {\"title\": \"US

\"highlights\": [\"# Message to the Congress Transmitting a Proposed Agreement for Cooperation Between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the United Arab Emirates
Concerning Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy\\n...\\nMay 21, 2009\\n...\\nI am pleased to transmit to the Congress, pursuant to sections 123 b. and 123 d. of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended
(42 U.S.C. 2153(b), (d)) (the \\\"Act\\\"), the text of a proposed Agreement for Cooperation Between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the United Arab Emirates
Concerning Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy. I am also pleased to transmit my written approval, authorization, and determination concerning the Agreement, and an unclassified Nuclear Proliferation
Assessment Statement (NPAS) concerning the Agreement. (In accordance with section 123 of the Act, as amended by Title XII of the Foreign Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act of 1998 (Public Law
105-277), a classified annex to the NPAS, prepared by the Secretary of State in consultation with the Director of National Intelligence, summarizing relevant classified information, will be submitted
to the Congress separately.) The joint memorandum submitted to me by the Secretary of State and the Secretary of Energy and a letter from the Chairman of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission stating the
views of the Commission are also enclosed.\\n...\\nThe proposed Agreement has been negotiated in accordance with the Act and other applicable law. In my judgment, it meets all applicable statutory
requirements and will advance the nonproliferation and other foreign policy interests of the United States.\\n...\\nThe Agreement provides a comprehensive framework for peaceful nuclear cooperation

\"Don\\u2019t Mistake a US-Saudi Nuclear Cooperation Agreement for a Nuclear Project - The National Interest\\n\\n# Don\\u2019t Mistake a US-Saudi Nuclear Cooperation Agreement for a Nuclear
Project\\n\\n August 17, 2026 By: Daniel Joyner\\n\\n## The agreement opens a carefully regulated legal pathway for American nuclear exports. It neither grants Saudi Arabia an enrichment capability
nor materially advances a Saudi weapons program.\\n\\nThe new US-Saudi nuclear cooperation agreement has had an unusually confusing debut.\\n\\nO\", \"highlights\": [\"On July 22, the United States
and Saudi Arabia signed an agreement for peaceful nuclear cooperation pursuant to Section 123 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended, 42 U.S.C. \\u00a7 2153. The agreement was accompanied by two
side letters and a separate arrangement providing for additional safeguards and verification measures. The package was then submitted to Congress for the review prescribed by the Atomic Energy
Act.\\n...\\nrocessing, enrichment,\\n...\\nBefore approving the Saudi agreement, Trump issued Presidential Determination No. 2026-18 on July 16. Exercising the authority conferred by Section 123(b),
he determined that performance of the proposed agreement \\u201cwill promote, and will not constitute an unreasonable risk to, the common defense and security.\\u201d\\n...\\nCongress may disagree
with that assessment as a matter of policy. But there is no persuasive basis for calling the agreement unlawful or in some manner improper merely because it does not contain every additional
nonproliferation commitment that its critics would prefer. Most importantly, Section 123 does not require every cooperating state to renounce every possibility of domestic uranium enrichment or spent-
fuel reprocessing, regardless of the origin of the relevant material, equipment, or technology.\\n...\\nThe new US-Saudi package also includes a separate Agreement for the Application of Additional
Safeguards and Verification Measures. Public reporting indicates that these measures would be implemented by the IAEA in connection with US-Saudi cooperation. The IAEA has stated that it is awaiting a
request from\\n...\\nand Riyadh before seeking authorization from its Board of Governors to implement them.\\n...\\nsafeguards. On\\n...\\nINFCIRC\\n...\\nFirst, does the agreement contain a Saudi-
wide renunciation of enrichment? Apparently, it does not. Unlike the UAE, Saudi Arabia has not agreed to forgo enrichment using any material or technology, regardless of its source.\\n...\\nThat
omission preserves Saudi Arabia\\u2019s juridical position that neither the NPT nor its comprehensive safeguards agreement categorically prohibits peaceful enrichment under safeguards. It does not,
however, confer access to American enrichment technology or eliminate US consent rights over material and equipment supplied pursuant to\\n...\\nSecond, does the 123 agreement itself authorize Saudi
Arabia to enrich uranium? Nothing publicly released demonstrates that it does. News reports indicate that the parties may conduct a two-year study of the technical and economic feasibility of
producing nuclear fuel in Saudi Arabia. But an agreement to study the feasibility of enrichment is not authorization to construct or operate an enrichment facility.\\n...\\nSection 123(a)(7) requires
prior US approval before nuclear material subject to an agreement for cooperation may be reprocessed or otherwise altered in form or content. In addition, 42 U.S.C. \\u00a7 2153a provides that, except
as specifically provided in an agreement for cooperation, source or special nuclear material exported from the United States may not be enriched after export without prior American approval. Proposals
involving enrichment could also implicate the subsequent-arrangement procedures of Section 131.\\n...\\nThird, does\\n...\\nagreement authorize the transfer of American enrichment technology? Again,
nothing publicly available establishes that it does. Authorization to transfer enrichment technology would present a distinct and\\n...\\nsensitive legal question. It could not be inferred from the
existence of a 123 agreement and would implicate the Atomic Energy Act\\u2019s special treatment of \\u201csensitive nuclear technology,\\u201d DOE authorization under Part 810, the Nuclear Suppliers
Group Guidelines, and potentially the subsequent-arrangement procedures of Section 131.\\n...\\ndoes not ordinarily export enrichment technology. Nothing about establishing\\n...\\nlegal framework
for\\n...\\nto begin doing so in\\n...\\nCongress should scrutinize the agreement carefully. It should demand publication and explanation of the two side letters and the additional safeguards
arrangement. It should determine how the administration complied with the procedural requirements imposed by Section 1264 of the 2020 National Defense Authorization Act. It should ask exactly what the
proposed enrichment study will examine, whether reprocessing is separately addressed, what happens if the United States ultimately refuses to support Saudi enrichment, and whether any future proposal
involving sensitive fuel-cycle technology will receive additional congressional consideration.\\n...\\nSection 123 opens a carefully regulated legal pathway for American nuclear exports. Parts 110 and
810, the subsequent-arrangement process, US consent rights, IAEA safeguards, and transaction-specific executive-branch review still determine what may pass through it.\\n...\\nThe agreement neither
grants Saudi Arabia an enrichment capability nor materially advances a Saudi weapons program. It permits American companies to seek participation in Saudi Arabia\\u2019s emerging nuclear market while
preserving the legal mechanisms through which the United States can approve, condition, or reject particular forms of cooperation.\"], \"published_date\": \"2026-08-17T09:13:52.964\", \"score\":

## 💭 Thinking



## 💬 Response

I have a complete dataset. Here is my synthesis.

# U.S. Section 123 Nuclear Cooperation Agreements: Timeline Base Rates, 2015–2026

## 1. The procedural pipeline — why "completion of negotiations" ≠ signature

The Atomic Energy Act sequence has five discrete gates, and the gap the question asks about sits between gates 1 and 3:

1. **Negotiations conclude / text agreed** (sometimes marked by initialing or a publicized "Joint Statement/Declaration on the Completion of Negotiations")
2. **U.S. interagency review** — State drafts the Nuclear Proliferation Assessment Statement (NPAS) + classified annex with DNI; DOE/NNSA concurrence; NRC views; partner completes its own domestic authorization
3. **Presidential Determination** under §123 b. approving the agreement and authorizing the Secretary of State "to arrange for its execution"
4. **Signature**
5. **Transmittal to Congress → 90 days of continuous session → entry into force** (absent a joint resolution of disapproval; Congress has never disapproved one)

The critical structural finding: **the Presidential Determination precedes signature by days, not months.** So the entire "completion → signature" delay is the gate-2 interagency/NPAS/domestic-approval bottleneck.

| Agreement | Presidential Determination | Signed | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| UK | Apr 30, 2018 (PD 2018-07) | May 4, 2018 | **4 days** |
| Mexico | Apr 30, 2018 (PD 2018-06) | May 7, 2018 | **7 days** |
| Singapore | Jul 26, 2024 (PD 2024-08) | Jul 31, 2024 | **5 days** |
| Thailand | Jan 10, 2025 (PD 2025-02) | Jan 14, 2025 | **4 days** |
| Saudi Arabia | Jul 16, 2026 (PD 2026-18) | Jul 22, 2026 | **6 days** |
| Vietnam | Feb 24, 2014 (PD 2014-08) | May 6, 2014 | 71 days |

Five of six are 4–7 days. A published Presidential Determination is therefore a near-immediate leading indicator of signature; Vietnam's 71 days is the sole exception.

## 2. Completion of negotiations / initialing → formal signature (the direct answer)

This is a **small n**, because most 123 agreements never have a separate public "completion of negotiations" event — they simply get signed.

| Case | Completion event | Date | Signed | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **South Korea** | Provisional/initialed pact signed in Seoul (Amb. Lippert / Park Ro-byug) | Apr 22, 2015 | Jun 15, 2015 | **54 d (1.8 mo)** |
| **UAE** | Final text agreed (~early Nov 2008) | ~Nov 5, 2008 | Jan 15, 2009 (Rice) | **~71 d (2.3 mo)** |
| **UAE (re-signature)** | same | ~Nov 5, 2008 | May 21, 2009 (Obama admin) | ~197 d (6.5 mo) |
| **Vietnam** | Initialed by Kerry & Pham Bình Minh, Brunei | Oct 10, 2013 | May 6, 2014 | **208 d (6.8 mo)** |
| **Saudi Arabia** | "Joint Declaration on the Completion of Negotiations," White House | Nov 18, 2025 | Jul 22, 2026 | **246 d (8.1 mo)** |
| **Armenia** | "Joint Statement on the Completion of Negotiations," Yerevan (Vance/Pashinyan) | Feb 9, 2026 | **not signed** | **191+ d (6.3+ mo), open** |

**Central tendency:** of the three completed cases with a clean public completion marker (ROK, Vietnam, Saudi), the median is **208 days ≈ 6.8 months**, mean ≈ 169 days. Including the UAE first-signature analog gives a median of ~140 days (4.6 months). The full observed range is **~2 to ~8 months**.

### The most important analytical caveat

**The existence of a separate, publicized "completion of negotiations" ceremony is itself evidence that signature is *not* imminent.** In every case where the U.S. was legally ready, it simply signed — Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, UK, Mexico, and Norway had no completion-of-negotiations event at all. The joint statement/declaration format appears to be used specifically when a high-level visit (MBS at the White House; Vance in Yerevan) needs a deliverable *before* the NPAS and domestic approvals are finished. Both instances of the formal "Joint Statement/Declaration on the Completion of Negotiations" construction — Saudi Arabia and Armenia — are Trump-administration-era and are the two slowest cases in the dataset.

The Armenia joint statement text is explicit that the delay is procedural: the governments "intend to proceed with their respective internal review and approval procedures, as well as any other legal steps, required prior to the signature and entry into force."

For comparison, where there was no completion ceremony, informal signals ran short: the Philippines was described as "90 percent done" by both the U.S. ambassador and the Philippine energy undersecretary in **September–October 2023** and signed **November 16, 2023** — roughly 2 months from "90% done" to signature, with the whole negotiation taking about seven months.

## 3. Signature → entry into force (n = 25, complete CRS dataset)

| Percentile | Days | Months |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum | 57 (India) | 1.9 |
| Median (all 25) | **232** | **7.6** |
| Median excl. 4 outliers >400 d | 199 | 6.5 |
| Median, post-2010 signatures (n=11) | 199 | 6.5 |
| Median, post-2010 excl. Mexico/UK (n=9) | **184** | **6.0** |
| Maximum | 2,868 (Turkey) | 94.2 |

Recent cases cluster tightly at 4.5–7.5 months: Singapore 134 d, Vietnam 150 d, ROK 163 d, Thailand 176 d, Taiwan 184 d, China 199 d, UAE 210 d, Norway 222 d, Philippines 229 d, Australia 232 d.

**The long tails are all partner-side or geopolitical, not congressional:** Mexico 1,640 d (4.5 yr, Mexican Senate), UK 972 d (2.7 yr, tied to Brexit), Russia 980 d, Turkey 2,868 d (7.8 yr). Congress has never disapproved a 123 agreement.

## 4. Renewals: are they signed well before expiry, or close to it?

**Answer: close to it, and sometimes not at all.** This is the most striking finding.

**Renewed in time (barely):**
- **China** — 1985 agreement expired Dec 30, 2015; successor signed Apr 13, 2015, transmitted Apr 21, EIF Oct 29, 2015 — **2 months of margin**.
- **Taiwan** — expired Jun 22, 2014; successor signed Dec 20, 2013, EIF Jun 22, 2014 — **EIF landed exactly on the expiry date**.

**Missed the original expiry, required a statutory bridge:**
- **South Korea** — 1974 agreement was to expire Mar 19, 2014. Negotiations (begun Oct 2010) failed to conclude, so Congress enacted a **two-year extension** (P.L. 113-81, Feb 12, 2014) to Mar 19, 2016. New agreement initialed Apr 2015, signed Jun 15, 2015, EIF Nov 25, 2015 — ~20 months *after* the original expiry.

**Lapsed outright, no successor:**
- **Colombia** — expired Sep 17, 2013.
- **Egypt** — expired Dec 29, 2021; DOE revoked Egypt's Part 810 generally-authorized status Jan 31, 2023.
- **South Africa** — the sharpest cautionary case. The 1995 agreement (EIF Dec 4, 1997) was to expire Dec 4, 2022. Successor negotiations began in 2018 and stalled over South Africa's insistence on the right to manufacture its own fuel. The U.S. approved a **4-year stopgap extension** — Presidential Determination 2022-21 (Aug 25, 2022), transmitted to Congress Sep 1–2, 2022 — but the transmittal letter noted it "will be executed once the Republic of South Africa completes its required domestic process." **South Africa never completed it; the agreement lapsed**, and the NRC suspended Westinghouse's Koeberg fuel export license on Jan 13, 2023. South Africa remains absent from the in-force list in 2026.

That last case is the key structural warning: **a 123 instrument can be fully approved by the President and transmitted to Congress and still fail to be signed/executed because the partner state doesn't complete its own procedures.**

**Renewals that require no negotiation at all:** agreements with automatic rolling extensions simply roll over — Morocco (expired May 16, 2021), Turkey (Jun 2, 2023), and Euratom (Apr 12, 2026, now running to 2031) all auto-renewed. Japan's expired Jul 17, 2018 and "remains in force until terminated by a Party." Where renewal terms are *not* specified, a wholly new agreement must be negotiated and submitted — the upcoming cases are **Argentina (Oct 16, 2027)**, Ukraine (2029), Brazil (2029), Kazakhstan (2029), Indonesia (2031).

**Long gaps after lapse are normal when a country isn't urgent:** Thailand's 1974 agreement expired June 2014; the successor was signed **Jan 14, 2025 — 10.5 years later**. The Philippines' predecessor expired in 1998; the successor was signed **Nov 16, 2023 — 25 years later**.

## 5. Current pipeline as of August 19, 2026

- **In force:** 26 agreements covering 50 countries + IAEA + Taiwan (NNSA, last updated Jul 11, 2025). Most recent additions: Philippines (EIF Jul 2, 2024), Singapore (Dec 12, 2024), Thailand (Jul 9, 2025).
- **Armenia** — negotiations completed Feb 9, 2026. **Still unsigned** at 6.3 months. Confirmed by an expert quoted in Caucasus Watch (Jul 29, 2026): the 123 Agreement "has yet to be signed and must then be ratified in the United States and likely in Armenia as well." Armenia's reactor-technology decision has meanwhile slipped to 2027 (Minister Khudatyan, Jun 11, 2026), reducing urgency.
- **Saudi Arabia** — signed Jul 22, 2026 (DOE; Arms Control Association dates Wright's signature Jul 23). **Transmittal status is contested**: Alhurra (Aug 4) and ACA (Aug 7) both reported it had *not* been sent to Congress, so the 90-day clock had not started; a National Interest analysis (Aug 17) states the package "was then submitted to Congress." Treat as unresolved. Sokolski (NPEC) estimated entry into force "sometime before the end of this year" if transmitted promptly.
- **Malaysia** — MOU signed Jul 10, 2025; Malaysia announced readiness to begin 123 negotiations, but as of Nov 2025 the Deputy PM said Malaysia was still "assessing whether it needs to sign" one. No negotiation completion.
- **Bahrain** — MOU only (Jul 2025). No 123 agreement.
- **South Africa** — lapsed since Dec 2022, negotiations deadlocked.
- **Poland** — covered by the Euratom agreement; no bilateral needed.

## 6. Data quality notes

- Media routinely conflate the two events. Bloomberg, Al Jazeera, DW, NucNet and ANS all headlined Armenia's Feb 9, 2026 joint statement as "signed a civil nuclear cooperation agreement" / "sign nuclear deal." World Nuclear News, Reuters, Public Radio of Armenia, and the Armenian PM's own office correctly describe it as a **joint statement on the completion of negotiations**. Bloomberg's own Nov 19, 2025 Saudi story is the clearest on the distinction: "A formal 123 Atomic Energy Act agreement... has yet to be signed, a US Energy Department spokesman confirmed."
- The authoritative structured source is **CRS RS22937, Appendix A, Table A-1**, updated Feb 10, 2026, which gives signature, EIF, duration, expiration, and renewal terms for all 25 bilateral agreements. NNSA's list gives EIF/expiration only (no signature dates).
- The CRS table's Korea row reads "November 24, 1972 (proposed renewal agreement signed June 15, 2015)"; the operative modern date is June 15, 2015.

## 💬 Response

I've completed the research. The findings are in my report above, with the structured data submitted.

**The headline answer to your question:** the gap from a publicized "completion of negotiations"/initialing to formal signature has run **~2 to ~8 months**, median ~6.8 months across the three clean completed cases (South Korea 54 days, Vietnam 208 days, Saudi Arabia 246 days). Armenia is currently open at 191+ days.

**Three findings worth flagging as the most decision-relevant:**

1. **The completion-of-negotiations ceremony is itself a negative signal for near-term signature.** Most 123 agreements never have one — Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, UK, Mexico, and Norway all went straight from finished text to signature. The formal "Joint Statement/Declaration on the Completion of Negotiations" construction appears exactly twice, both Trump-era (Saudi Arabia, Armenia), and both are the slowest cases in the dataset. It looks like a device for giving a high-level visit a deliverable before the text is legally ready.

2. **The Presidential Determination is the real leading indicator** — it precedes signature by 4–7 days in five of six observed cases. That is the event to watch, not diplomatic statements.

3. **Renewals run close to the wire and sometimes fail.** China had two months of margin; Taiwan's entry into force landed exactly on the expiry date; South Korea missed its original expiry and needed a two-year act of Congress. Three agreements have lapsed outright. The South Africa case is the strongest caution for the Armenia situation: a stopgap extension was approved by Presidential Determination and transmitted to Congress in September 2022, yet was never executed because South Africa didn't complete its domestic procedures — and the agreement lapsed, costing Westinghouse its Koeberg export license.

**Two caveats on the data:** the Saudi congressional transmittal status is genuinely contested — Alhurra (Aug 4) and the Arms Control Association (Aug 7) both said it had not been sent, while a National Interest analysis (Aug 17) says it had. I could not resolve this and have reported it as unresolved rather than picking a side. Separately, mainstream media (Bloomberg, Al Jazeera, DW, NucNet, ANS) all reported Armenia's February joint statement as a signed 123 Agreement; only World Nuclear News, Reuters, and the Armenian PM's own office got it right. Any resolution source drawing on general news coverage may encode that error.
